title: Art History · Episode 3
chapters: The Bauhaus: the school that designed the modern world

units.t: Art History. Episode three.
In this episode: Impressionism, Modern art, explained and The Bauhaus: the school that designed the modern world.
Part one. Impressionism.
Rejected by the art establishment and mocked by critics, a group of painters in 1870s Paris changed how the world sees light.
Rejected by the Salon.
In 19th-century Paris, an artist's career depended on the Salon, the official exhibition run by the state-backed Académie des Beaux-Arts.
Its juries favoured large, highly finished paintings of history, myth and religion, with smooth surfaces that hid the brushwork.
Thousands of works were rejected each year.
In 1863 so many were turned away that Emperor Napoleon III allowed a Salon des Refusés, an exhibition of the rejected.
Crowds came partly to laugh, especially at Édouard Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe, which showed a naked woman picnicking with clothed men in modern dress.
Going it alone.

Frustrated with the Salon, a group including Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Camille Pissarro and Berthe Morisot organised their own show in 1874, in the former studio of the photographer Nadar.
One of Monet's works was titled Impression, Sunrise, a hazy view of the port of Le Havre.
The critic Louis Leroy seized on it and mockingly called the group 'Impressionists', meaning their pictures looked like unfinished sketches.
The artists eventually adopted the name.
They held eight group exhibitions between 1874 and 1886.
Painting light outdoors.
Traditional painters sketched outside but finished their pictures in the studio.
The Impressionists wanted to capture a real moment of light and weather, so many worked en plein air, French for 'in the open air'.
Paint in collapsible metal tubes, invented in 1841, made colours portable, and new railways carried Parisians to riverside towns and the coast.
Working fast before the light changed, they used quick, visible brushstrokes and set bright colours side by side, letting the eye blend them.
Monet painted the same subject at different times, such as haystacks and Rouen Cathedral, and later painted his Giverny water garden about 250 times.
A radical break.
Today Impressionism is hugely popular, but it broke several rules at once.
The paintings looked unfinished.
Their subjects were train stations, boating parties and gardens, not gods or battles, and they told no moral story.
Shadows were blue and purple rather than brown and black.
Japanese woodblock prints and photography influenced their cropped, flat, frozen compositions.
The painters were not all alike.
Renoir loved joyful social scenes.
Degas disliked the label and worked mostly indoors, painting dancers and cafés from odd angles.
Morisot, in seven of the eight shows, painted women and children at home.
Mary Cassatt, an American, also joined.
The Australian bush.
In the late 1880s, Melbourne painters including Tom Roberts, Arthur Streeton and Frederick McCubbin set up artists' camps at Box Hill and Heidelberg, then on the city's rural edge.
Painting outdoors, they tried to capture the harsh, bright Australian light.
In 1889 they held the 9 by 5 Impression Exhibition, with many works painted on cigar-box lids.
Roberts's Shearing the Rams, 1890, became a national icon.
Historians debate how closely they followed French Impressionism.
To enjoy these works, look from two distances.
Up close you see separate dabs of colour.
A few metres back they merge into shimmering light.
The key idea: In 19th-century Paris the state-run Salon decided which art was seen, and it favoured polished, traditional paintings.
Part two. Modern art, explained.
Melting clocks, soup cans and paint dripped on the floor: the ideas behind a century of art that people love to argue about.
Beyond copying the eye.
By the 1880s, some artists felt Impressionism was too focused on fleeting light.
The critic Roger Fry later grouped them as 'Post-Impressionists'.
Paul Cézanne rebuilt nature from simple shapes, aiming for solidity.
Vincent van Gogh used swirling brushwork and intense colour to express emotion, as in The Starry Night, 1889; he sold very few paintings in his lifetime.
Paul Gauguin used flat, symbolic colour.
Georges Seurat built pictures from tiny dots of pure colour, a method called pointillism.
Each moved away from copying the visible world and towards expressing ideas and feelings.
Cubism and abstraction.
Since the Renaissance, European painting used perspective to show a scene from one fixed viewpoint, like a window.
Around 1907 to 1914, Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque broke that rule.
They split objects into facets and showed several sides at once.
Cubists also invented collage, gluing newspaper onto canvas.
A painting was now a flat object, not a window.
That opened a question: could art show nothing recognisable at all?
In the 1910s Kandinsky compared colour to music, Malevich painted a black square, and Mondrian used straight lines and primary colours.
Hilma af Klint had painted abstractly since 1906 but kept it private.
In 1917 Duchamp submitted a urinal titled Fountain, asking what makes something art.
Dreams and the unconscious.
After the horror of World War I, many artists distrusted reason itself.
In 1924 the French writer André Breton published the Surrealist Manifesto, inspired by Sigmund Freud's ideas about dreams and the unconscious.
Surrealists tried to unlock the irrational through dream imagery, chance and automatic drawing.
Salvador Dalí's The Persistence of Memory, 1931, with its melting clocks, is the most famous example.
René Magritte painted a pipe with the words 'This is not a pipe' beneath it, a witty reminder that a picture of a thing is not the thing.
Surrealism spread into film, photography and advertising.
New York and Pop.
After World War II, the art world's centre shifted from Paris to New York.
Abstract Expressionists made huge canvases meant to carry intense feeling.
Jackson Pollock dripped and poured paint onto canvas laid on the floor, so the work recorded his movement.
Mark Rothko painted glowing rectangles of colour.
In 1973 the Australian government bought Pollock's Blue Poles for $1.
3 million, causing a public uproar.
It is now valued at far more.
In the late 1950s and 1960s, Pop Art reacted against that seriousness, borrowing from advertising, comics and celebrities.
Andy Warhol painted Campbell's Soup Cans, 1962, and Roy Lichtenstein enlarged comic panels, asking whether high art and commercial images were really separate.
My kid could do that.
The complaint that a child could paint a Rothko or a Pollock misses what these artists were doing.
Many were highly trained: Picasso painted in a skilled academic style as a teenager, then chose to abandon it.
The point was often the idea, the risk of going first, and hundreds of deliberate choices about scale, colour and balance.
A 2011 study found that people, including non-experts, more often preferred abstract artists' works over similar-looking pictures by children or animals.
When you meet a puzzling work, ask what the artist is rejecting, what choices you can see, and how it feels.
You are allowed not to like it, but try to understand it first.
The key idea: Post-Impressionists such as Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin and Seurat moved from copying what the eye sees towards expressing ideas and feelings.
Part three. The Bauhaus: the school that designed the modern world.
A German art school lasted only fourteen years before the Nazis shut it down.
Yet its ideas are in your kitchen chairs, your fonts and the buildings you walk past every day.
Art meets craft.
In 1919, just after the First World War, the architect Walter Gropius founded a school in Weimar, Germany, by merging an art academy with a school of arts and crafts.
He called it the Staatliches Bauhaus, roughly meaning state house of building.
Gropius believed the old split between fine artists and craftspeople was harmful.
Painters looked down on furniture makers, while industry churned out poorly designed products.
At the Bauhaus, students learned artistic principles and hands-on skills in workshops for metal, wood, textiles, pottery, printing and more.
The long-term goal was building, bringing all the arts together.
Germany was poor and divided, and the school hoped to help shape a better society.
Learning to see again.
New students first took the preliminary course, developed by Johannes Itten and later run by László Moholy-Nagy and Josef Albers.
The aim was to unlearn old academic habits and experiment directly with materials.
Students explored the textures of wood, glass, paper and metal, studied contrasts of light and dark, and built structures from folded paper.
Albers later became famous for his studies of how colours change depending on their neighbours.
The painters Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky taught theories of form and colour.
It was one of the most remarkable teaching staffs ever gathered.
Objects and women.
The school shifted from handcraft towards designing prototypes for industry.
Marianne Brandt designed teapots and lamps.
Marcel Breuer designed a tubular steel armchair in the mid 1920s, later called the Wassily chair, inspired by the steel tubes of his bicycle.
Herbert Bayer designed clean lower case typefaces.
Many Bauhaus designs are still made today.
The school officially welcomed women, and in its first year more women than men applied.
Leaders worried, and many women were pushed towards weaving.

They turned that limitation into an achievement: under Gunta Stölzl, the first female master, the weaving workshop became one of the most commercially successful, and Anni Albers developed new textiles.
Brandt broke into metalwork.
Dessau and the Nazis.
Conservative politicians in Weimar saw the Bauhaus as foreign, left-wing and a waste of public money, and cut its funding.
In 1925 it moved to Dessau, where Gropius designed an icon of modern architecture, completed in 1926: a glass curtain wall, flat roofs and linked wings.
Gropius stepped down in 1928, followed by Hannes Meyer and, from 1930, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe.
The Weimar and Dessau buildings are now UNESCO World Heritage sites.
The Nazis attacked it as un-German and communist.
After they gained power on Dessau's council, the school was forced out in 1932.
Mies tried to continue in Berlin, but police raided it, and the staff closed it in 1933.
Jewish and left-wing members suffered persecution, and some were killed in the Holocaust.
A worldwide legacy.
In fourteen years the school had perhaps 1,250 students, a small number for such influence.
Its closure scattered its ideas worldwide.
Gropius taught at Harvard, and Mies led the architecture school at what became the Illinois Institute of Technology, designing glass and steel towers that defined the modern skyline.
Moholy-Nagy founded the New Bauhaus in Chicago in 1937.
Josef and Anni Albers taught at Black Mountain College in North Carolina.
Bauhaus-trained architects helped build the White City of Tel Aviv, now a World Heritage site.
A common myth credits the Bauhaus with the slogan form follows function, but it came from the American architect Louis Sullivan in the 1890s.
Still, it suits the Bauhaus well.
The key idea: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in 1919 to unite art and craft, so students learned both principles and hands-on skills.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did the Salon juries mostly favour?
Answer. Large, polished paintings of history and myth.
Question two. What did Post-Impressionists such as Cézanne and Van Gogh move towards?
Answer. Expressing ideas and feelings over appearances.
Question three. What was Gropius's central aim for the Bauhaus?
Answer. To unite fine art and craft, working towards building.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
